title: How do you design this service to be highly available?
summary: Tests whether "high availability" means something concrete to you — redundancy, health checks, automated failover — rather than a buzzword attached to any design.

slides.markdown:
"Make it highly available" is one of the easiest phrases to say and one of the hardest to actually deliver — this question checks whether it means specific mechanisms to you or is just a buzzword you attach to any design that has more than one server.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to name the three concrete pillars — redundancy, health checks, automated failover — and describe exactly how each one works, at each layer of a system.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: what's the target, and what does an outage cost?
slides.markdown:
Ask **what target availability matters here** — 99.9% and 99.99% imply very different engineering investment (roughly 43 minutes vs 4.3 minutes of downtime/month). Then ask **what an outage actually costs** — lost revenue per minute, SLA penalties, or just user annoyance — since that cost is what justifies the investment.

A target with no stated cost of missing it is just a number; tying it to a real consequence is what makes the rest of your answer land as engineering judgment rather than a wish list.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: redundancy, health checks, automated failover
slides.markdown:
The skeleton, and the three things a strong answer names concretely: **redundancy** at every layer (no single unreplicated component), **health checks** to actually detect when something has failed, and **automated failover** to act on that detection without a human in the loop.

All three are required together — redundancy without health checks means you don't know something died; health checks without automated failover mean a human has to notice and act, which is far slower than the outage itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: N+1 redundancy at the app tier
slides.markdown:
**N+1 (or N+2) redundancy** means running more app instances than the minimum needed to serve current load, behind a load balancer with health checks — so losing one (or two) nodes still leaves enough capacity to serve traffic without a visible dip.

The "+1" isn't waste, it's the whole point: it's capacity you're deliberately not using day-to-day, purely so a failure doesn't turn into an outage. Sizing it (N+1 vs N+2) is a direct trade of idle cost against how many simultaneous failures you can absorb.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a DB primary-replica pair with automated failover
slides.markdown:
A **primary-replica database pair** with automated failover: a monitor watches the primary's health, and on detecting failure, promotes the replica and redirects traffic — without waiting for a human to be paged and respond.

Name the **failover-detection window** honestly: there's always a gap between the primary actually failing and the monitor being confident enough to promote the replica (to avoid false positives from a brief blip). That window is real downtime, even in an "automated" failover.

![Two availability zones each with their own load balancer, app instances, and database replica, connected by cross-AZ replication, noting that losing one AZ still leaves the other serving traffic](assets/multi-az-ha.svg)

**Multi-AZ placement** spreads redundant copies of every layer across physically separate data centers, so a single data-center-level failure (power, networking, a natural disaster) doesn't take down the whole service the way it would if every redundant copy sat in the same building.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: higher targets need multi-region
slides.markdown:
| Target | Typical architecture | What it trades |
|---|---|---|
| 99.9% | Redundancy within one AZ, automated restarts | Cheapest, vulnerable to a full AZ outage |
| 99.99% | Multi-AZ, automated failover | Higher cost, survives an AZ failure |
| 99.999% | Multi-region, active-active or active-passive | Highest cost, and often weaker consistency (cross-region replication lag) |

**How to decide:** each step up in target availability typically means going multi-region, which trades cost and often consistency (replication lag between regions) for uptime — name that trade before committing to a target.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the health check says healthy but the service is degraded
slides.markdown:
This is the gap between a **shallow health check** (does the process respond to a ping) and a **deep health check** (can the process actually serve a real request end-to-end, including its own dependencies). A service can pass a shallow ping while its database connection is exhausted and every real request is failing.

The fix: health checks should exercise a genuine, lightweight version of the real workload — not just confirm the process is running — so "healthy" actually means "capable of serving traffic."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how fast does failover actually happen, and what does the user see?
slides.markdown:
Name real numbers, not "it's automated so it's instant." A typical automated database failover might take 10-30 seconds from failure to a promoted replica serving traffic — during that window, in-flight requests fail or hang, and new requests may error until the promotion completes and routing updates.

Saying "users see a brief error or retry prompt for roughly N seconds" is a stronger, more credible answer than implying automated failover is seamless.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: calling a design "highly available" because it "has a load balancer"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** having a load balancer in the diagram is sufficient to call a design highly available.

**Why it's wrong:** a load balancer alone says nothing about whether the load balancer itself is redundant, whether health checks are deep enough to catch real degradation, or whether failover is automated versus requiring a human page — "highly available" is a property of the whole design's redundancy and detection, not one component's presence.

**Correct model:** be ready to name the redundancy, health-check depth, and failover mechanism at every layer — LB, app, database — not just point at a diagram and call it done. See [availability and reliability](availability-and-reliability) for the underlying mechanics.
